Psalms 47:2: "a great King over all the earth" (KJV), in a psalm sung in Israel's worship.
Revelation 11:15: "the kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord" (KJV).

Premillennialists say Christ's present reign is from heaven, while Zechariah 14 describes a visible reign on earth, with nations sent to Jerusalem yearly (14:16-19). They note that judgments on nations who do not come imply a world not yet perfect, fitting a millennium. Amillennialists apply 14:9 to Christ's present reign and the new creation.
What are the "living waters" flowing from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8)?
On the fulfilled reading, they picture the Spirit and the gospel going out from Jerusalem to the world after Pentecost, as Jesus promised.

Zechariah 14:8 says living waters will flow from Jerusalem, half to the eastern sea and half to the western sea, in summer and winter. Ezekiel saw a river flowing from the temple that brought life wherever it went (Ezekiel 47:1-12). Jesus said that from the believer's heart would flow rivers of living water. John explains that he spoke of the Spirit (John 7:37-39). He also offered the Samaritan woman living water (John 4:10-14). At Pentecost the Spirit was poured out in Jerusalem, and the gospel went out to Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). On the fulfilled reading, this is the flow of Zechariah 14:8. Read this way, the stream never stops, "in summer and in winter".
John 7:38-39: rivers of living water, "this spake he of the Spirit" (KJV).
Acts 1:8: witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth.

Futurists expect a real river flowing from a renewed Jerusalem in the millennium, as Ezekiel 47 describes. Amillennialists often apply the waters to the gospel age and to the river of life in the new creation (Revelation 22:1). Many interpreters see more than one layer of fulfilment.
What about the nations going up yearly to keep the Feast of Tabernacles (Zechariah 14:16-19)?
Futurists see a future millennium. The fulfilled reading sees the nations joining God's worship in Christ, in the language of Israel's harvest feast.

Zechariah 14:16 says survivors from the nations will go up each year to worship the King and keep the Feast of Tabernacles. Nations that do not go will have no rain. This text is not discussed in the source argument, but it is central for futurists. On the fulfilled reading, the prophets often describe the gospel age in the language of their own worship. Isaiah said foreigners would offer sacrifices on God's altar (Isaiah 56:6-7). Malachi said incense would be offered in every place (Malachi 1:11). Jesus said true worship would no longer be tied to Jerusalem (John 4:21-23). Tabernacles was the great harvest feast. Read this way, the nations gathered into Christ's harvest are its fulfilment (John 4:35; Revelation 7:9).
Malachi 1:11: incense offered "in every place" among the nations.
John 7:2, 37: Jesus gave the living-water promise at the Feast of Tabernacles.

Premillennialists say this text strongly supports a future earthly kingdom. People still live on earth, nations exist, and some disobey and are punished. They say this cannot be the eternal state or the present age. Amillennialists read it as a picture of worldwide worship, using the forms Zechariah's first readers knew.
Montanus and the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla (Phrygia)

Claimed new revelations from the Paraclete. Taught that the New Jerusalem would soon come down at Pepuza in Phrygia. The movement began between about 156 and 172 (Epiphanius and Eusebius give different dates).

The city never descended. Maximilla reportedly said no prophet would come after her and the end would follow. She died about 179, and the end did not come. Church synods in Asia rejected the movement (Eusebius, Church History 5.16).
Hippolytus of Rome (writing about AD 204)
Dated creation to 5,500 years before Christ and taught a 6,000-year world history. This placed the end about AD 500. He partly meant this to calm believers who expected the end immediately.
AD 500 passed without the end. Later writers moved the 6,000-year mark forward several times.
Popular expectation around the year 1000 in Western Europe
Some believers expected Satan to be released or the end to come at the close of a thousand years after Christ, or after his passion (1033).
No end came. Historians debate how widespread the fear was; the chronicler Rodulfus Glaber reports unrest, but later stories of mass panic are often exaggerated.
Followers of Joachim of Fiore (died 1202)
Joachim taught three ages of history. His followers calculated that the Age of the Spirit would begin about 1260, after 42 generations of 30 years.
Nothing changed in 1260, though flagellant processions spread through Italy that year. A Joachite work by Gerard of Borgo San Donnino was condemned in 1255.
Thomas Müntzer and armed peasant bands (Germany)
Preached that the godly must take the sword to prepare for Christ's kingdom and that God would protect them in battle.
His army was crushed at Frankenhausen on 15 May 1525. Müntzer was captured and executed on 27 May 1525.
Melchior Hoffman (Strasbourg)
Proclaimed that Christ would return in 1533 and that Strasbourg would be the New Jerusalem.
Hoffman was jailed in Strasbourg in 1533 and died in prison about 1543. No return took place.
Jan Matthys and Jan of Leiden (Münster, Westphalia)
Declared Münster the New Jerusalem. Matthys predicted judgment on the ungodly at Easter 1534.
Matthys was killed in a sortie on Easter Sunday, 5 April 1534. Jan of Leiden ruled as king until the city fell on 25 June 1535. The leaders were executed in January 1536.
In his Book of Prophecies (about 1501-1502) he reckoned that about 155 years remained before the end of the world.
The year 1656 passed without the end.
John Napier (Scottish mathematician)
In 1593 he calculated from Revelation that the day of judgment would fall between 1688 and 1700.
Both dates passed. Napier is remembered today for inventing logarithms, not for his date.
William Miller and the Millerite movement (United States)
Miller taught that Christ would return "about 1843" (21 March 1843 to 21 March 1844), based on the 2,300 days of Daniel 8:14 as years from 457 BC. Samuel Snow then fixed 22 October 1844.
The "Great Disappointment" of 22 October 1844. Many left the faith; others formed new groups, including Seventh-day Adventists, who reinterpreted the date as Christ entering the heavenly sanctuary.
Charles Taze Russell and the Bible Students (later Jehovah's Witnesses)
Taught that the "Gentile Times" would end in October 1914, bringing the end of human governments and the full kingdom of God.
The First World War began, but the present world order did not end. Russell died in 1916. The movement later taught that Christ began ruling invisibly in heaven in 1914.
J. F. Rutherford, Watch Tower president
In "Millions Now Living Will Never Die" (1920) he said 1925 would see the return of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and other faithful men of old.
Nothing happened in 1925. Rutherford later admitted the expectation was mistaken. Attendance fell sharply in the following years.
Watch Tower Society (Jehovah's Witnesses)
Its 1966 book "Life Everlasting in Freedom of the Sons of God" placed the end of 6,000 years of human history in autumn 1975, and leaders spoke of the millennium being near.
No change came in 1975. Membership declined in the following years, and in 1980 the Watchtower acknowledged that expectations had been wrongly raised.
Herbert W. Armstrong, Radio Church of God
His booklet "1975 in Prophecy!" (1956) and the church's preaching led members to expect great tribulation in the early 1970s and Christ's return about 1975.
1975 passed. The church later stressed that no exact date had been set.
Pat Robertson, television broadcaster
In 1980 he told viewers that he could "guarantee" a judgment on the world by the end of 1982.
No such world judgment came in 1982.
Hal Lindsey, The Late Great Planet Earth (1970)

Linked the fig tree (Matthew 24:32) to Israel's rebirth in 1948 and suggested a generation is "something like forty years". Readers took this to mean the rapture by about 1981 and Christ's return by about 1988. His 1980 book called the 1980s possibly "the last decade".
1988 passed. Lindsey later said a generation might be 60 to 80 years and avoided a fixed date.
Edgar C. Whisenant, "88 Reasons Why the Rapture Will Be in 1988"
Said the rapture would occur at the Feast of Trumpets, 11-13 September 1988. Millions of copies were distributed.
Nothing happened. He blamed a one-year calendar error and moved the date to 1989, then to later years. Each new date failed.
Dami Mission, led by Lee Jang-rim (South Korea)
Announced that the rapture would take place on 28 October 1992. Some followers quit jobs and gave away property.
No rapture came. Lee Jang-rim was convicted of fraud in December 1992 after police found he had invested followers' money in bonds maturing in 1993.
Harold Camping, Family Radio, "1994?" (1992)
Calculated from a creation date of 11,013 BC that the end would very probably come in September 1994.
September 1994 passed. Camping said he had made a calculation error.
Y2K and year-2000 prophecy writers (e.g. Lester Sumrall, Grant Jeffrey)
Some said human history would be complete by 2000. Others said the "millennium bug" computer crisis would set the stage for the Antichrist's world government.
The year 2000 arrived with only minor computer problems. No world government or end-time crisis followed.
Announced the rapture and a great earthquake for 21 May 2011, and the destruction of the world on 21 October 2011. Billboards were placed in many countries.
Neither date brought the end. Camping retired after a stroke, and in March 2012 Family Radio said he had been wrong to set a date.
Mark Biltz and John Hagee, "blood moons"
Linked the four total lunar eclipses of 15 April 2014, 8 October 2014, 4 April 2015 and 28 September 2015, on Passover and Tabernacles, to a coming world-changing event affecting Israel.
The tetrad passed without any such event. Similar tetrads have occurred many times in history without prophetic meaning.
David Meade, writer on "Planet X"
Claimed that a sign in the stars on 23 September 2017 (read from Revelation 12) would begin end-time events, including a hidden planet near earth.
Nothing happened. NASA had stated that no such planet exists. Meade then shifted his claims to later dates.

First imperial persecutor of Christians (AD 64). "Neron Kesar" in Hebrew letters adds to 666, and the Latin form gives 616, a variant reading in Revelation 13:18. A legend said he would return from death.
Caligula (Gaius)
In AD 40 he ordered his statue set up in the Jerusalem temple (Josephus, Antiquities 18.8; Philo). He was killed before it was done.
He demanded divine honours and is often linked with persecution in Asia. Tertullian said he had "a portion of Nero's cruelty" (Apology 5).
Muhammad, or the power of Islam
Innocent III linked the 666 of Revelation 13:18 to the years of Islamic rule and expected its end to be near. The view was polemical and arose in a time of war.
Emperor Frederick II
In a bitter church-state conflict, the pope called him the beast rising from the sea. Frederick's side replied by calling the pope the Antichrist.
The papacy
The man of lawlessness sits in "the temple of God", read as the church. The pope claimed to stand in Christ's place as his vicar. Many later Protestants have dropped this view.
By assigning number values to the Latinised name "Martin Lutera", writers produced 666, a sign of how easily the method can be turned against anyone.
Napoleon Bonaparte
His conquests and his titles were read as 666 in Roman numerals, and "Apollyon" (Revelation 9:11) was linked to "Napoleon".
Benito Mussolini
He spoke of reviving the Roman Empire, seen as the beast's healed head. The slogan "VV IL DUCE" was said to equal 666 in Roman numerals.
Adolf Hitler
His war, cruelty and genocide of the Jews. Writers made his name equal 666 by starting the alphabet at A = 100.
Joseph Stalin
Leader of an atheist state that persecuted churches; Russia was linked with "Gog" in Ezekiel 38.
John F. Kennedy
A charming leader who received a fatal head wound, linked to the beast's "deadly wound" (Revelation 13:3). The idea ignored that the wound in the text is healed.
Henry Kissinger
As US Secretary of State he arranged Middle East agreements, read as the "covenant" of Daniel 9:27. Some claimed his name had a value linked to 666.
King Juan Carlos I of Spain
He was crowned in 1975, and the Spanish crown holds the old title "King of Jerusalem". He was linked to a revived European empire.
Mikhail Gorbachev
A world peace-maker with a mark on his forehead; he was welcomed in Israel in 1992. Writers claimed numerical values for his name.
Ronald Wilson Reagan
Each of his three names has six letters. His retirement home address was 666 St. Cloud Road (changed to 668). The 1981 assassination attempt was linked to the beast's wound.
Saddam Hussein
He rebuilt parts of ancient Babylon and invaded Kuwait in 1990, which was read as a sign of Babylon's return (Revelation 18).
Charles, Prince of Wales (now King Charles III)
His heraldry, his name values and his talk of uniting faiths were read as signs. Such claims have no grounding in the biblical text.
Barack Obama
His popularity, his peace language and claims about his background. These were partisan claims, not biblical study.
Who did the speaker first address?
Look for "you", named churches, places or groups. Matthew 24 speaks to disciples in Judea. Revelation 2-3 speaks to seven named churches.
A specific first audience ("you", a named city or church)
God's people in general, with no clear time frame
What time words does the text contain?
Words such as near, shortly, at hand, about to, quickly, this generation, some standing here. Or long words such as "many days" or "the time of the end".
Near words: soon, at hand, this generation
Far words: "many days", "sealed until the time of the end"
No time words at all
Does a later text say that the far-off time has now arrived?

Daniel was told to seal his vision because it was for "many days" (Daniel 8:26; 12:4). John was told not to seal his, because "the time is near" (Revelation 22:10). The New Testament also speaks of "the end of the ages" coming (1 Corinthians 10:11; Hebrews 9:26).
Yes, a later text says the time has come
No later text marks it as near
Where does the picture language come from?

Compare the Old Testament. Darkened sun and falling stars were used for the fall of Babylon, Edom and Egypt (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Ezekiel 32:7). Coming on clouds was used of God judging Egypt (Isaiah 19:1).
Stock Old Testament judgment imagery
Language of final resurrection: all the dead raised, death itself ended
Is there a documented event within the stated time frame that matches?
Check the New Testament itself (Acts), then Josephus, Tacitus and Eusebius. Ask whether the match is close and specific, not loose.
Yes, a close match (e.g. Jerusalem's siege and fall, AD 66-70)
Partly; some details fit and others are disputed
No event in that time frame fits
Does the passage also state a lasting principle?
Many fulfilled prophecies still teach: God judges covenant-breakers, protects those who heed his word and keeps his promises (1 Corinthians 10:11).
Yes, it states a principle that applies in every age
No, it is tied to that one event
What kind of text is it?
Some prophetic texts are commands or promises for every age. Some describe the whole stretch between Christ's first and second comings. Some describe the end of history.
A command, warning or promise about how to live
A picture of the kingdom's growth or the church's life in this age
A picture of the end of history: resurrection, final judgment
Does the New Testament treat this as the final goal of all history?
Look for the resurrection of all the dead, the end of death, the last judgment of every person, and God being "all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:24-28; Acts 17:31; Revelation 20:11-15).
Yes, it describes the final consummation
It describes an ongoing process rather than one final event
I cannot tell yet
Is the time frame itself clear?
If the time words are clear but the historical match is disputed, keep the time frame and keep studying the history. If the time frame is unclear, hold your view humbly.
The time frame is clear
The time frame is unclear
Fulfilled in the first century

On the fulfilled reading, this text was for its first hearers and came to pass within their lifetime, most often in the events of AD 66-70. Futurists may see a second, later fulfilment; weigh whether the text itself signals one.
Fulfilled, with a lasting lesson
The event is past, but the principle it shows still applies. Read it as history that warns and comforts, as Paul read the wilderness story (1 Corinthians 10:11).
An ongoing principle
This text tells God's people in every age how to live: watch, endure, repent, love and work. It does not need a date to apply today.
Symbolic of the whole present age
This text pictures the life of Christ's kingdom from his ascension to his return: growth, conflict, witness and suffering. Idealist and amillennial readers find much of Revelation here.
Still future: the final consummation
Nearly all Christians, including partial preterists, agree that the bodily resurrection, the final judgment and the end of death are still ahead (Acts 17:31; 1 Corinthians 15:24-28).
Hold it humbly and keep studying
The evidence is not clear enough to decide. Compare the texts again, read several views, and do not build a timetable on it (Acts 1:7).
What does Jesus say must happen before "this generation" passes away (Matthew 24:34)?
Only the first few signs
"All these things" he had just described
Nothing, since the phrase means the Jewish race
Jesus says "all these things" would happen before that generation passed. The fulfilled reading links them to AD 70. Futurists read "generation" as a later generation or as a race.
Which Gospel explains the "abomination of desolation" as Jerusalem surrounded by armies?
Mark
Luke
John
Luke 21:20 says, "When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation is near." Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14 speak of the abomination in the same place in the discourse.
In what year did Roman forces burn the Jerusalem temple?
AD 64
The temple burned in August AD 70 under Titus (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-6.5.1). AD 64 was the fire of Rome; AD 135 ended the Bar Kokhba revolt.
Where do the words "the sun will be darkened" and "the stars will fall" first appear as judgment language on a nation?
In the Old Testament prophets, for example on Babylon
Only in Revelation
In Josephus
Isaiah 13:10 uses this language for Babylon's fall to the Medes. Isaiah 34:4 and Ezekiel 32:7 use it for Edom and Egypt.
According to Eusebius, where did Jerusalem's Christians flee before the siege?
Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3, says the church in Jerusalem was warned to move to Pella in Perea before the war.
Where does the word "antichrist" appear in the Bible?
Only in 1 and 2 John
In Daniel and Revelation
In 2 Thessalonians
The word is found only in 1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3 and 2 John 7. John defines it as anyone who denies that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh, and he says "many antichrists" were already present.
Which name, spelled in Hebrew letters, adds up to 666?
Neron Kesar (Nero Caesar)
Titus Flavius
Julius Caesar
Nrwn Qsr = 50+200+6+50+100+60+200 = 666. The Latin form without the final n gives 616, a reading found in some manuscripts of Revelation 13:18.
Where else in the Bible does the number 666 appear?
Solomon's yearly gold (1 Kings 10:14)
The size of Noah's ark
The age of Methuselah
Solomon received 666 talents of gold a year (1 Kings 10:14; 2 Chronicles 9:13), just before his decline into idolatry. Ezra 2:13 also lists 666 descendants of Adonikam.
What did William Miller's followers experience on 22 October 1844?
The founding of a new state
The "Great Disappointment"
A great earthquake
Christ did not return on the date Samuel Snow had fixed from Daniel 8:14. The non-event became known as the Great Disappointment.
Which date did Harold Camping give for the rapture in 2011?
11 September 2011
21 December 2011
Camping named 21 May 2011 for the rapture and 21 October 2011 for the end of the world. Both passed, and he later withdrew from date setting.
What does Acts 1:7 teach about dates?
They can be calculated from Daniel
It is not for us to know times or seasons the Father has set
The end will come within forty years
Jesus told the apostles that the Father has fixed times by his own authority. This stands against date setting in every age.
What does Revelation 1:1 say about the events it shows?
They will happen after many ages
They "must shortly come to pass"
They are only symbols with no time
Revelation 1:1 and 22:6 say the events must "shortly" take place, and 1:3 and 22:10 say "the time is near". Readers differ on how to take these words, but they must be explained.
Why was Daniel told to seal his vision, while John was told not to seal his?
Daniel's was for "many days"; John's time was near
Daniel wrote in Aramaic
John wrote to Gentiles
Daniel 8:26 and 12:4 seal a vision for a distant time. Revelation 22:10 says, "Do not seal up the words... for the time is near."
Which phrase best describes "newspaper exegesis"?
Reading current events into the Bible
Comparing Scripture with Scripture
Studying ancient historians
It means reading the Bible through today's headlines. Its long record of failed identifications warns against it.
Which document named the Pope as "that Antichrist" in 1646?
The Nicene Creed
The Westminster Confession of Faith
Westminster Confession 25.6 named the Pope as Antichrist. Many Reformed churches have since revised or removed this clause.
In the fulfilled reading, what is the "fig tree" lesson of Matthew 24:32-33?
Israel's rebirth in 1948
Seeing the signs means the judgment is near, at the door
A sign of a coming harvest festival

Jesus uses the fig tree as a simple lesson: when leaves appear, summer is near. So when the disciples saw the signs, the end of the age was near. Luke 21:29 adds "and all the trees", which weakens a special link to Israel.
Which Old Testament text does Jesus quote when he speaks of "coming on the clouds" before the high priest?
In Matthew 26:64 Jesus joins Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13. Daniel pictures the Son of Man coming to the Ancient of Days to receive a kingdom.
What do almost all Christians, including partial preterists, still expect in the future?
The bodily resurrection and the final judgment
A seven-year treaty with Israel
Partial preterists affirm, with the creeds, a future bodily return of Christ, the resurrection of the dead and the final judgment (Acts 17:31; 1 Corinthians 15:24-28).
